rv.q: Lauryn Ajufo’s magnetic and irrepressible performance makes Michaela Coel’s darkly comic monologue completely her own

Lauryn Ajufo takes the character out of the shadow of the TV series to make Tracey her own – more pugnacious, earnestly schoolgirlish yet also streetwise, her youthful fears mixed with a child's dead-eyed cruelty.
Ajufo is so strong in this one-woman play that it seems impossible that another actor could ever play the cheeky Black schoolgirl who naively believes she's streetwise.
Ajufo is a firecracker on stage.

Standing once as a beacon of what was to come for Michaela Coel, the show now stands as proof of her undeniable legacy, as well as a breathtaking showcase for another up-and-comer in Lauryn Ajufo's finely-tuned performance.
His production, with partner company Tiata Fahodzi, is a really invigorating experience.

cn.t: Michaela Coel's 2012 debut monologue proves timeless in this vibrant Theatre503 revival, with Lauryn Ajufo's powerhouse performance capturing the comedy and confusion of adolescence while demonstrating the play's enduring relevance.
